lignes.texte: Big Tech is chasing record profits by culling its human workforce so AI can step into the void.
Except that’s not what’s happening… at least not at Meta.
Deep inside a corporate boardroom, Mark Zuckerberg is panicking.
Hours before a secretive project was due to launch a brutal purge of engineers,
Zuckerberg pulled the plug. Something had gone catastrophically wrong. A ruthless C suite plan
had pushed one of the world’s most profitable companies to the brink of an internal meltdown.
And now, Zuckerberg is trapped in the fallout.
The chaos brewing at Meta has been a long time coming. And it’s a warning for any company looking
to axe their headcount and replace it with AI. It all came to a head in May 2026, when over
8,000 engineers lost their jobs. It was a massive number, roughly 10% of Meta’s entire workforce.
And it was just the start.
But while Zuckerberg and his high paid executives were planning their purge,
Meta’s systems were beginning to fracture.
Tech and security issues had surged by 40%. Overwhelmed engineers were taking
70% longer just to keep the platform online. The culprit was the company’s active AI agents,
which were making changes to live code. With no human oversight,
the agents were running amok. No one could track the changes at the scale they were being made.
Just weeks earlier, Zuckerberg had told his staff that the integration
of AI tools was not the driver of upcoming layoffs. He refused to say the real reason,
leaving his workforce completely in the dark.
Then the leaks came.
Katie Paul, an investigative journalist at Reuters, was the one to reveal the truth.
Paul exposed the real story through internal documents, and confidential
sources within Meta. Those leaks revealed the sheer brutality of Zuckerberg’s plan,
which was based on a blueprint called the “AI Native Guide”.
The document outlined a full corporate restructuring called
“Project OT”, or Organizational Transformation.
The scheme was hatched at Zuckerberg’s Hawaii compound, during his annual leadership retreat.
And it wasn’t about cost cutting.
The goal was to erase the workforce.
Autonomous AI agents would replace thousands of employees, removing the need for engineers,
project managers and designers. The remaining workers would be
formed into small teams that would oversee the agents. They
would be forced to hit targets while handling more work than was feasible.
But this was just the beginning.
Meta’s plan was much bigger.
Project OT would go global. It would be sold to other corporations and
businesses across the world to help them eliminate their staff.
Zuckerberg had seen the future and human employees weren’t part of it.
Well, at least not in his vision of it.
The eradication of human workers was pitched on every slide at the meeting
on the Hawaii compound. Meta had the money. It had the structure. And more importantly,
it had the guinea pigs. 2 billion daily users to test their master plan on. The executives believed
that if autonomous agents could replace engineers anywhere on earth, it would happen here first.
But pitching on a slide is one thing.
Doing it in real life is something else.
By June 2026, Zuckerberg’s gamble was starting to fail. And the evidence was in Meta’s code.
Chief Technical Officer Andrew Bosworth posted a metric to internal staff. According to Bosworth,
Meta saw 220% increase in code changes to internal platforms and infrastructures. But
when it came to the actual features reaching users, the number stood at a paltry 36%. There
was a tripling of code changes resulting in practically zero product improvement.
And this issue isn’t confined to Meta.
It’s the dirty little secret of the AI industry.
Back in July 2025, research group METR conducted a groundbreaking study. They
recruited 16 experienced developers and gave them almost 250 coding tasks. Then,
they flipped a coin to decide to see if they could use AI tools or code manually.
Before the testing, the developers estimated that AI would make them 24% more productive.
In reality, it made them 19% less productive.
The psychological results were even more alarming. After the study finished,
the developers genuinely believed that AI had made them about 20% faster.
They were about 40% slower and didn’t even realize it.
That blind spot was the reason for Meta’s 220% system overload. When code is generated
by a push of a button, it creates the illusion of speed. A senior engineer will spend about
45 minutes tweaking and modifying an AI prompt that they could have
produced themselves in 12 minutes. All while swearing the tool saved time.
Industry data proves this.
GitClear, an analytics firm that monitors live production codebases,
reported that after AI tools spread, copy-pasted code grew by about 400%. At the same time,
they reported a 60% drop in the work of cleaning up and simplifying old code.
Zuckerberg’s vision of an automated paradise was actually a bloated,
rapidly growing digital monster that was spiraling out of control.
Anthropic, the lab behind Claude, ran a separate study on junior developers. Those who relied on
AI to help them scored 17% lower on their ability to explain code snippets to their
peers. The sheer volume code changes created a mountain of additional work for other engineers.
They were trapped in a dystopian feedback loop.
They were using AI tools to review code changes that were written by AI,
using review software that was also written by AI. The volume of reviews skyrocketed,
the quality tanked, and increased the chance of errors. Meta engineers were
forced to work twice as hard to catch bugs that weren’t written by human developers.
Project OT was meant to break this loop.
Instead, it just accelerated it.
And in February 2026, Andrew Bosworth poured fuel on this AI dumpster fire.
He publicly claimed that Meta’s top engineer puts his annual salary into tokens and gets a 10 times
return. In response, a Meta engineer created an internal dashboard that listed over 85,000
employees by who burned through the most A.I. tokens. This dashboard, dubbed Claudeonomics,
publicly ranked the top 250 users and gave them titles such as Token Legend and Session Immortal.
Suddenly, burning tokens became the ultimate metric for performance reviews. In one month, Meta
employees burned a total of 60.2 trillion tokens, and the top user burned 281 billion tokens alone.
Neither Zuckerberg nor Bosworth made the Top 250.
60.2 trillion tokens equals an approximate public model price of $900 million. Meta probably pays
less, but engineers believe the true price is in the range of $100 to $200 million.
That’s the budget of a Triple A video game. But there was no physical product,
nothing that users could enjoy. The cash came from the same pot the upcoming
layoffs was supposed to protect. While no one was forced to compete,
the leaderboard warped the company’s behaviour. A metric became a performance target. At that point,
it became worthless. For decades, have failed at quantifying programmers by lines of code. Bloated,
messy engineers were rewarded while the ones who wrote clean code were penalized.
Meta repeated that mistake.
Engineers began using AI on simple tasks that could have been done by hand. They
didn’t want to look like anti-AI employees. Once the leaderboard went up, the company’s
priorities were clear to everyone. Company wide token usage skyrocketed to 73.7 trillion,
and it continued to increase even after growing media pressure caused it to be scrapped.
The toxic behaviour became embedded in the culture.
It took until June for Andrew Bosworth to send out a memo to 6,000 employees about the misuse
of AI tools. He reminded staff that just because they could use AI, it didn’t mean they had to.
The sentiment was right.
But it was months too late.
The message landed months after token burning had already determined who was productive and
who was replaceable. It took them another 3 months to change the review criteria. So,
for a quarter, ratings were based on the old behavior.
But even though AI models could not solve complex problems, this did not slow down
Meta’s efforts. They started looking for training data on employees’ computers.
They harvested staff click and keystroke data to show agents how the workforce
functions. Staff still had to hit productivity outputs while a machine watched and learned.]
Then the employees fought back.
Protest flyers started to be hung around the workspace, criticising the keystroke
surveillance. The blowback was so severe, Meta put it on hold, provided exemptions,
and said that employees could opt out in the future. A few flyers hung in a
shared kitchen brought down a multi-million dollar automation program. The keystroke
surveillance never ran in the UK, where the laws on watching staff are tighter.
Same company, same agents, different rules.
The resistance worked.
Zuckerberg’s master plan to aggressively downsize the engineering team was sabotaged by his own
staff. Some engineers who had been forced on to AI teams were allowed to return to their old jobs.
But the psychological damage had already been done.
In just 6 months, Meta’s internal Pulse surveys showed a 19 point
drop. Staff flooded internal forums with pictures of elephants. The joke
being the elephant in the room that the leadership team refused to acknowledge.
Andrew Bosworth said that in the 20 years he had spent working at the company,
morale had probably never been lower. He told engineers the people in charge had
done an atrocious job of explaining the vision.
In July 2026, Zuckerberg admitted what many had already guessed. The
“agentic path” had stalled. He was still claiming that autonomous AI capabilities
were 3 to 6 months away. It’s a target that has been recycled for 2 years,
and it’s not any closer to being reached. Every quarter the breakthrough is estimated
to be 6 months out, and spending is approved in the meantime.
Broken code and staff revolts were the reason the second wave of cuts were frozen. But that
doesn’t explain why a bigger, second wave was ever scheduled in the first place.
The answer lies in the numbers.
Meta has two huge expenses: People and Computing. They can’t increase spending
on one without trimming the other. It’s not a complex business philosophy, it’s reality.
In 2024, Meta spent $39.2 billion on capital expenditures. By 2025,
it had nearly doubled to $72.2 billion. 2026 was a completely different beast.
Zuckerberg and his team jacked up Meta’s annual infrastructure budget to $145 billion.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Meta locked themselves into $107 billion worth
of multi-year infrastructure contracts. They were buying up long lead items like power,
land, buildings, and next generation microchips.
Meta’s 2026 spending completely eclipses their total spending for 2024 and 2025 combined.
And it seems to be working.
Second Quarter 2026 Revenues increased 28% to $60.8 billion, the strongest growth in 5
years. Despite this impressive growth, advertising revenues were up only 27%.
But those headline figures mask the truth.
Capital expenditures in the quarter more than doubled to $31.1 billion, cannibalizing the
company’s liquid cash. Free Cash Flow saw a 91% decline from the same quarter last year.
When the unexpected infrastructure bills landed,
Meta’s share prices plummeted. It tanked 10% in after hours trading.
To keep the lights on, Meta did something unprecedented.
It went on a borrowing spree. The company issued nearly $25
billion of long-term debt, causing their total debt to hit $83.66 billion. Worst,
they halted their buyback scheme of shares. Instead of returning cash to shareholders,
like they did every year, they ploughed it into the machine..
Meta’s Net Property and Equipment surged to $225 billion, an increase of almost $50
billion in just 6 months. They also leased an additional $68 billion of data center space,
with a total of $279 billion of such leases still to be fulfilled.
It’s a lot of money regardless of whether the AI actually works.
They’re also designing their own custom AI chip, Iris, to help them reach gigawatt
scale compute capacity by September 2026. None of this can be put on hold.
The steel has already been ordered, and power contracts have already been signed.
So the bills will start coming regardless.
A hiring plan can change in the span of an afternoon. A gigawatt
of power locked into a 10 year contract can’t.
In the second quarter of 2026, Meta cut 8,000 jobs and spent over $1 billion on
severance pay.. Bank of America estimates the cuts could save the company between $7 billion
and $8 billion a year. That covers roughly three weeks of a $137.5 billion buildout.
Three weeks.
Employees were replaceable. Departments could be cut along with the people in
them because the infrastructure timeline couldn’t.
Investors were concerned about margins because all that spending was pushing
profits further away. When asked about returns over the next 12 to 24 months,
Zuckerberg avoided the question. He said it was too technical. It wasn’t really an answer.
It was a CEO buying time when he didn’t have much left.
Project OT was designed to save the company’s profit margins by executing the staff,
while protecting the real investment. But things began to quickly unravel because of
the code the AI agents wrote and the product that users received.
In August 2026, Zuckerberg wrote an essay about AI. He argued that in his estimation,
AI would create more jobs than it would eliminate. But 2026 was also the year
he axed 8,000 jobs and shuttered 6,000 open positions. It was when he reorganized teams
to a fraction of their previous sizes. All of this happened within a 90 day window.
His essay was PR.
And the data contradicted it.
Meta is the biggest example of a company trying to automate jobs out of existence. It’s the company
the tech industry will be watching closely. It’s a tech giant with deep pockets, taking giant leaps
with huge proposals. Meta designs and builds its own data centers, creates its own AI, and recruits
the top engineers. The vast majority of companies will never be in the same position as Meta.
Sure, it can spend $130 billion in a single year on computing power. Yet, even with infinite
resources it still needed human workers to check the mistakes made by its AI agents. In fact,
Meta’s agents made so many mistakes that Meta brought those human workers back.
The next company to try this won’t be a tech company. It could be a bank,
an insurance company, or a hospital system. Somewhere, an executive is probably looking
at a slide that shows a decrease in engineers with no change in output. That
entire corporate strategy sits on the belief that Big Tech has already proven it works.
But Zuckerberg hasn’t proved anything. Meta only survived because it stopped
hours before the second round of layoffs. And it hid the truth for another 3 months.
But this experiment has already played out in public.
Klarna, the Swedish payments company, revealed in February 2024 that it had
replaced 700 customer service agents with an OpenAI assistant. It said AI agents handled
over two thirds of all customer chats. The CEO of Klarna, Sebastian Siemiatkowski,
believed he had the technology to replace human jobs. After that announcement,
the company put in a company wide hiring freeze which lasted for over a year.
It was big talk.
And it didn’t stand up.
By 2025, Klarna was hiring people again. Siemiatkowski admitted that the company had
gone too far with its cost cutting. Chasing profit had resulted in a poor product,
and customers had the right to talk to a real person.
This happened two years before Zuckerberg's Hawaii
meeting. Anyone building Project OT could have looked it up.
But Zuckerberg still believes in his vision of the future.
The one where workers are replaced by agents.
But those agents will still be 6 months away, as they always are.
AI has already started to change how software gets built, driven by a staggering amount of
generated code. But no one has answered the question. What happens when a company that
does not have $60 billion in quarterly revenue makes the same bet and cuts the same people?
Meta can make mistakes in public and keep paying
the employees who remained. That is how it got to change its mind.
Other companies only get to make one big mistake.
